# Choosing Between Free Transit, Congestion Pricing, and Cycle Lanes to Cut Commuter Car Trips 20% in Three Years

## Why the question is harder than it looks

The stated goal — cut *commuter car journeys* by 20% in three years — is more specific than it sounds. It is not "reduce emissions," "cut congestion," "improve equity," or "grow transit ridership." Those four goals are what free transit, congestion pricing, and cycle lanes are usually justified by, and all three interventions can look successful against them while doing very little to the actual metric in question. A city that makes transit free and sees ridership jump 14% has not necessarily put a single car driver on a bus — if most of those new riders used to walk, the emissions and equity numbers can improve while the car-commute number barely moves. Any serious analysis has to keep the metric narrow and interrogate each intervention specifically against *car trips*, not against the adjacent goals it's more commonly sold on.

It's also worth flagging, before anything else, that "cut commuter car journeys by 20%" is not yet a fully specified target. Does "commuter" mean only home-to-work trips, or all work-related travel? Does "car journey" mean solo drivers only, or does a carpool passenger count as removed? Is 20% measured against current trip counts or current mode share, and is it a relative cut (20% fewer of today's car trips) or an absolute one (a 20-point mode-share shift)? None of this is specified, and a city that doesn't pin it down before choosing an intervention will not be able to tell, three years later, whether it succeeded. This has to be fixed at the same time the intervention is chosen, not after.

## 1. Is "choose one" a false framing?

Largely, yes — and recognizing this is the single most important move in the whole analysis.

The three interventions are not actually substitutes for each other; they act on different parts of the same system. Congestion pricing acts directly on the decision to drive. Free transit acts on the cost of one alternative. Cycle lanes act on the quality/safety of a different alternative. Nothing about how any of them works prevents doing all three, and in the two best-documented real-world implementations of congestion pricing (Stockholm and London), the pricing was not deployed in isolation — Stockholm in particular ran an expanded public transport rollout before the charge went live, and virtually every large-scale pricing scheme funds transit or active-travel improvements from its own revenue. The "pick one of three" framing in the question is a convention baked into how the choice was posed, not a real constraint any physical or legal fact imposes.

Running the numbers on a weighted comparison across the realistic options — pricing alone, free transit alone, cycle lanes alone, doing nothing, and a sequenced bundle led by pricing and funded transit/cycling investment — the bundled strategy outscores every single-lever option on every criterion that isn't a tie (mechanism strength, effect size, fiscal sustainability, political durability, robustness across city types, and equity), and this result is robust: there is no plausible single change to how those criteria are weighted that flips the ranking back to any single-lever option. Pricing alone comes closest, but it loses specifically on the two axes — political durability and equity — that a well-designed bundle is built to fix.

So the honest answer is: **default to a bundle**, not a single pick. But that doesn't mean "do all three at full intensity everywhere." The real decision a city needs to make is not *which one* but *how to sequence and weight the three*, and that weighting is genuinely context-dependent — which is what the decision framework in section 3 is for.

The one condition under which "choose exactly one" becomes the right frame is genuine scarcity of implementation capacity: a city with very limited political capital, budget, or administrative bandwidth that can only credibly execute one major transportation policy change in three years. In that narrower case, the choice really does collapse to picking the single highest-expected-value lever — and the analysis below is built so that case falls out of the same framework as a special case, rather than needing a separate answer.

## 2. Mechanism, requirements, and failure modes — intervention by intervention

### Free public transit (fare elimination)

**Mechanism:** Removes the cost of the substitute. It only reduces car trips to the extent that the specific people who take advantage of free fares were previously driving.

**What has to be true for it to work against this metric:** The city needs an existing base of drivers who are meaningfully price-sensitive about the fare itself (not just indifferent to transit because it's slow or infrequent), and the transit system needs enough spare capacity to absorb a ridership surge without degrading service.

**Where it fails or backfires against this specific metric:** The best-documented real-world case of a fare-free rollout (Tallinn, Estonia) found that transit use jumped sharply, but car use fell only modestly — and walking trips collapsed by nearly 40%. In other words, the people most responsive to a fare cut were disproportionately former pedestrians and cyclists, not drivers. Worse, average car-trip distances *increased* even as the car-use share dipped slightly, meaning the net effect on vehicle-miles was arguably negative. This is the single clearest empirical illustration in this whole analysis of the goal-conflation problem: free transit is a genuinely strong lever for accessibility, equity, and ridership — and a weak, slow, and uncertain one for the specific metric of commuter car trips. There's also a structural risk that compounds over time: transit agencies typically fund 30–60% of their operating costs from fares, so eliminating them opens a large, permanent budget hole with no revenue engine behind it. If that hole isn't backfilled from elsewhere, service quality degrades over the following years, which can *increase* car use rather than reduce it — the opposite of the goal, arriving on a delay.

### Congestion pricing

**Mechanism:** Attaches a direct cost to the trip being measured. Unlike the other two interventions, it doesn't depend on anyone discovering or adopting a substitute first — the price acts on the car trip itself.

**What has to be true for it to work:** A definable zone or corridor that can be priced and enforced, and — critically — enough capacity on the alternatives (transit, bikes, carpooling) to absorb the people who stop driving, or a large enough population for whom eliminating the trip entirely (working from home, rescheduling, trip-chaining differently) is viable.

**Evidence:** Two independent, well-documented implementations — Stockholm's 2006 trial and London's 2003 charge — each produced double-digit reductions in vehicle trips within the priced zone, in the range of roughly 18–25%, measured within the first year of charging and, in Stockholm's case, sustained for many years after. This is the strongest, fastest-materializing, most directly-targeted mechanism of the three against exactly the metric in question. In fact, a 20% target sits comfortably *inside* the range that pricing alone has already demonstrated elsewhere — it is not an aspirational reach past known results, it's calibrated almost exactly to them.

**Where it fails or backfires:** Two failure patterns dominate, and neither is really about the mechanism itself. First, **capacity crowding**: if transit can't absorb the diverted trips, pricing just pushes people into an overcrowded alternative rather than a workable one, and the backlash from that degrades political support. Second, and more seriously, **political reversal**: pricing is the most politically fragile of the three interventions once implemented. New York City's congestion pricing program is the sharpest illustration — the plan took roughly six years from enabling legislation to actual launch, was indefinitely postponed by the governor days before it was set to start, and only survived because it was revived at a lower price point months later. A charge that drives off exemptions to placate affected businesses, or that has its revenue quietly redirected away from the transit/bike investments that were supposed to make it durable, can be functioning perfectly as an economic mechanism and still get killed politically before its effect on the metric ever gets measured. There's also a geographic caveat specific to the "mid-sized" framing: London, Stockholm, and NYC all have a legible, dense downtown zone that's easy to price. A more sprawling mid-sized city without a clear single destination may need a different zone design (corridor tolling, cordon around multiple activity centers) for the mechanism to bite at all.

### Protected cycle lanes

**Mechanism:** Improves the quality and safety of an existing substitute (cycling), making a bike a more viable choice for trips that were previously made by car.

**What has to be true for it to work:** This is the one intervention whose ceiling is set by geography rather than policy design. A commute trip has to fall within a rider's practical range — roughly 5–8 kilometers for a typical unassisted trip, extending somewhat further with e-bikes and cargo bikes — for a bike lane to even be a structural candidate for replacing that trip. Climate and topography matter directly here too: extreme heat, cold, or hills materially shrink the population willing to make the switch even when the distance is short enough. And a single protected corridor rarely does much on its own — cycling uptake depends heavily on network connectivity, i.e., whether a rider can get from home to work on protected infrastructure the whole way, not just for one segment.

**A rough sizing check, done honestly with wide brackets rather than false precision:** even under fairly optimistic assumptions — a third to half of all commute trips falling within cycling range, and 5–15% of that reachable population actually switching within three years (accounting for the fact that a network built over three years is partial, not complete) — the arithmetic works out to something like a 1–8 percentage-point contribution to the 20% target. That's a real, valuable contribution, but nowhere close to sufficient on its own under any defensible set of assumptions. Cycle lanes are also the slowest to compound: individual corridors can open within a construction season, but the network effect that actually drives ridership only shows up once enough of the network is connected, which typically takes multiple years even in well-resourced programs.

**Where it fails or backfires:** In a city with long average commute distances, harsh climate, or hilly terrain, cycle lanes can be built well, on budget, on schedule, and still contribute almost nothing to the car-trip metric — not because of poor execution, but because the geography was never a good match for the tool. This is the most likely intervention to be chosen for the wrong reasons (it's popular, it's visible, it photographs well) in a city where it structurally cannot move the needle much on this specific goal.

## 3. The decision framework — which structural variables route the choice

Rather than a single universal answer, the choice (or more precisely, the *weighting and sequencing* of the three levers) should be set by five structural facts about the city:

**1. Baseline car-commute mode share and existing transit capacity headroom.** A city with a high car-mode-share and a transit system running well below capacity has the most room to run pricing hard, because the displaced trips have somewhere to go. A city whose transit system is already crowded at peak needs capacity investment *before* or *simultaneously with* any lever that relies on transit as the release valve — otherwise it just relocates the problem into overcrowded buses and trains.

**2. Density, geography, and the commute-distance distribution.** This is what determines how much weight cycling can carry. A compact city with short average commutes and mild climate can lean harder on a connected cycle network as a meaningful contributor. A sprawling, hilly, or climate-extreme city should discount cycling's expected contribution sharply and lean more heavily on pricing and transit capacity instead — building bike lanes there may still be worthwhile for other goals, but shouldn't be counted on to move this metric much.

**3. Existing bike-network connectivity.** A city that already has partial bike infrastructure can complete a connected network faster and see returns sooner than one starting from zero; this shifts cycling from "long-shot, low-priority" to "worth accelerating."

**4. Fiscal capacity and farebox dependency.** A transit system heavily dependent on fare revenue (as most are) makes free transit fiscally dangerous unless the city has another funding source lined up in advance — otherwise the "free" policy quietly turns into a service-quality problem within a few years. Conversely, a city with slack in its budget, or one willing to dedicate pricing revenue to transit, can afford to be more ambitious.

**5. Political capital, existing legal authority, and equity exposure.** A city that already has home-rule authority to levy a zone charge (versus one that would need new state legislation) can move on pricing much faster — this alone can be the difference between pricing launching within the three-year window or not. A city with a large low-income, car-dependent population needs equity design (income-based rebates, not blanket exemptions) built into the pricing scheme from day one, or the political coalition supporting it will erode.

**How this cashes out in practice, as a rule of thumb:**

- **High car-mode-share, underused off-peak transit, a legible corridor or downtown, and existing legal authority to price:** lead with congestion pricing, backed by pre-committed revenue recycling into transit and bikes. This city can move fastest and has the strongest mechanism available.
- **Long average commutes, harsh climate, dispersed job centers:** downweight cycling's expected contribution; lean harder on pricing plus transit capacity to do the heavy lifting.
- **Weak political capital, no existing tolling authority, or a legislature likely to be hostile:** don't anchor the strategy on pricing in year one. Sequence transit-capacity investment and cycle-network build-out first (both can start immediately with mostly local authority), while building the legal case for pricing in parallel, accepting a longer runway to the full 20% and being honest that the first year or two will show a smaller effect.
- **Large low-income, transit- or car-dependent population:** whichever levers are chosen, equity design has to be explicit and structural (rebates over exemptions, expanded off-peak transit coverage) rather than an afterthought, because it's both a fairness issue and a durability issue — the mitigations that protect low-income drivers are the same ones that keep the political coalition behind pricing intact.

## 4. How the three-year window actually constrains this

The three interventions sit at very different points on a "speed to implement" vs. "strength of mechanism" trade-off, and none wins on both dimensions:

- **Free transit** can be switched on in a single budget cycle — months, not years — because it requires no new infrastructure or legal fight. But per section 2, it's also the slowest and weakest to actually move the car-trip metric, and it creates a compounding fiscal liability that can make things worse by year three if unaddressed.
- **Cycle lanes** can open individual corridors within a single construction season, but a network large enough to produce a meaningful mode shift typically takes multiple years of sequential build-out — realistically consuming most or all of a three-year window just to reach partial connectivity.
- **Congestion pricing's** bottleneck is almost never physical construction (the camera and tolling infrastructure itself is comparatively fast to install) — it's the legal and political runway. In the hardest documented case, a major city's pricing program took nearly six years from enabling legislation to actual launch, including a near-total political cancellation along the way. A city with existing legal authority to levy a charge could move far faster than that; a city that needs new state-level enabling legislation should assume the authorization process alone could eat a large share of the three-year window.

The practical implication: **don't wait for one lever to finish before starting the next.** The reason the bundled, sequenced approach outperforms any single-lever approach isn't just that it's more effective — it's that it lets a city work on multiple time-scales simultaneously. Transit-capacity and cycle-lane construction can start immediately using existing municipal authority and start producing partial results in year one, while the legal and political groundwork for pricing proceeds in parallel rather than in sequence. This is also the single best insurance against the scenario where the three-year clock runs out on the slowest-moving piece before anything is live.

## 5. Key failure scenarios and how to guard against them

Running a structured pre-mortem on the recommended bundled/pricing-anchored approach — imagining it has already failed by year three — surfaces six clusters of risk, each of which needs a specific answer, not a general reassurance:

**Authorization and lead-time risk.** The single biggest threat to the whole three-year timeline is that legal and political authorization for pricing consumes most of the window before the charge is even live — this is exactly what happened in the worst documented real-world case. *Mitigation:* secure or confirm legal authority and start enforcement-technology procurement in parallel with, not after, transit-capacity work. If authorization genuinely can't happen within the window, the honest fallback is to lead with capacity and cycle-lane investment and add pricing in year two or three rather than promising it as the anchor from day one.

**Capacity-sequencing risk.** If transit capacity isn't expanded ahead of or alongside the charge, the people who stop driving crowd an already-full system, reproducing the same failure pattern that undermines free-transit-alone strategies. *Mitigation:* make the pricing go-live date conditional on a published, binding capacity threshold (a specific bus-frequency or rail-headway target) being met first — turn "backfill capacity" from an intention into an operational gate.

**Measurement and definitional risk.** Without an agreed definition of "commuter car journey," a baseline, and a measurement method, the city can make real progress and still be unable to prove it in year three — and that ambiguity itself becomes a political liability. *Mitigation:* define the metric, baseline, and measurement approach in the enabling policy itself, before launch, so success or failure is falsifiable.

**Political-durability and revenue-integrity risk.** A charge's revenue-recycling promise can be quietly redirected during a budget shortfall, or a change in city administration can reverse or water down the program before its effects fully materialize — again, this has actually happened in the largest, best-resourced real-world example. *Mitigation:* this risk can't be fully engineered away, but it can be structurally reduced by legally earmarking revenue into a locked account rather than a routine budget line, so redirecting it requires a separate, visible political act rather than a quiet decision.

**Exemption-erosion risk.** Affected businesses and interest groups lobbying for exemptions can shrink the priced population enough to fall well short of the demonstrated effect before any measurement dispute even arises. *Mitigation:* use income-based rebates administered after the fact rather than blanket category exemptions — this preserves the price signal for the general driving population while still protecting the people who genuinely need protection.

**Legitimacy-shock risk.** A single visible operational failure early on — a billing glitch, a confusing zone boundary, a traffic-diversion incident — can end political support for the whole program regardless of how sound the underlying design is. *Mitigation:* run a phased or reduced-charge trial period specifically to surface and fix operational problems while the political cost of failure is still low, accepting a short delay to full effect in exchange for a much lower risk of an early, high-visibility failure.

## 6. Recommendation

Don't select a single intervention. Run a **pricing-anchored, revenue-recycled, sequenced program**: congestion pricing supplies the core mechanism because it's the only one of the three that acts directly on the metric being measured and has real-world evidence landing right inside the 18–25% range the city is targeting; its revenue pre-funds transit-capacity expansion and a connected cycle-lane network; and the relative weight and sequencing of the three levers — how hard to lean on cycling, how fast to move on pricing, how much capacity to build first — is set by the five structural facts about the specific city: its baseline car-mode-share and transit headroom, its density/geography/commute-distance profile, its existing bike-network connectivity, its fiscal capacity and farebox dependence, and its political capital and equity exposure.

The key insight worth carrying forward is that the question's own framing — pick one of three — is itself the biggest hidden assumption in the whole decision, and it doesn't survive scrutiny: free transit's mechanism acts mainly on people who weren't driving in the first place, cycle lanes' ceiling is set by a geographic fact most cities can't change in three years, and a weighted comparison of all the realistic strategies shows a bundled, pricing-anchored program beating every single-lever option on nearly every criterion, robustly enough that no reasonable change in how those criteria are weighted reverses the result.

The honest trade-off to acknowledge: anchoring on pricing buys the strongest and fastest mechanism at the cost of the weakest political-durability and equity profile of the three raw levers, and the mitigations needed to fix that (revenue earmarking, income-based rebates rather than blanket exemptions, capacity-first sequencing) will themselves shrink the realized effect somewhat below the best-case 18–25% range — meaning a well-designed program should expect to land nearer the lower half of that range, not its ceiling, especially in its first year or two. And regardless of which combination is chosen, the city cannot actually verify whether it hit "20%" until it defines what that number means — which trips count, what baseline it's measured against, and whether it's a relative or absolute figure — so that definitional work has to happen at the same time as the intervention decision, not after the fact.

Political capital, existing legal authority, and equity exposure.** A city that already has home-rule authority to levy a zone charge (versus one that would need new state legislation) can move on pricing much faster — this alone can be the difference between pricing launching within the three-year window or not. A city with a large low-income, car-dependent population needs equity design (income-based rebates, not blanket exemptions) built into the pricing scheme from day one, or the political coalition supporting it will erode.

- **High car-mode-share, underused off-peak transit, a legible corridor or downtown, and existing legal authority to price:** lead with congestion pricing, backed by pre-committed revenue recycling into transit and bikes. This city can move fastest and has the strongest mechanism available.
- **Long average commutes, harsh climate, dispersed job centers:** downweight cycling's expected contribution; lean harder on pricing plus transit capacity to do the heavy lifting.

- **Large low-income, transit- or car-dependent population:** whichever levers are chosen, equity design has to be explicit and structural (rebates over exemptions, expanded off-peak transit coverage) rather than an afterthought, because it's both a fairness issue and a durability issue — the mitigations that protect low-income drivers are the same ones that keep the political coalition behind pricing intact.

## 4. How the three-year window actually constrains this

The three interventions sit at very different points on a "speed to implement" vs. "strength of mechanism" trade-off, and none wins on both dimensions:

- **Free transit** can be switched on in a single budget cycle — months, not years — because it requires no new infrastructure or legal fight. But per section 2, it's also the slowest and weakest to actually move the car-trip metric, and it creates a compounding fiscal liability that can make things worse by year three if unaddressed.
- **Cycle lanes** can open individual corridors within a single construction season, but a network large enough to produce a meaningful mode shift typically takes multiple years of sequential build-out — realistically consuming most or all of a three-year window just to reach partial connectivity.
- **Congestion pricing's** bottleneck is almost never physical construction (the camera and tolling infrastructure itself is comparatively fast to install) — it's the legal and political runway. In the hardest documented case, a major city's pricing program took nearly six years from enabling legislation to actual launch, including a near-total political cancellation along the way. A city with existing legal authority to levy a charge could move far faster than that; a city that needs new state-level enabling legislation should assume the authorization process alone could eat a large share of the three-year window.

The practical implication: **don't wait for one lever to finish before starting the next.** The reason the bundled, sequenced approach outperforms any single-lever approach isn't just that it's more effective — it's that it lets a city work on multiple time-scales simultaneously. Transit-capacity and cycle-lane construction can start immediately using existing municipal authority and start producing partial results in year one, while the legal and political groundwork for pricing proceeds in parallel rather than in sequence. This is also the single best insurance against the scenario where the three-year clock runs out on the slowest-moving piece before anything is live.

## 5. Key failure scenarios and how to guard against them

Running a structured pre-mortem on the recommended bundled/pricing-anchored approach — imagining it has already failed by year three — surfaces six clusters of risk, each of which needs a specific answer, not a general reassurance:

**Authorization and lead-time risk.** The single biggest threat to the whole three-year timeline is that legal and political authorization for pricing consumes most of the window before the charge is even live — this is exactly what happened in the worst documented real-world case. *Mitigation:* secure or confirm legal authority and start enforcement-technology procurement in parallel with, not after, transit-capacity work. If authorization genuinely can't happen within the window, the honest fallback is to lead with capacity and cycle-lane investment and add pricing in year two or three rather than promising it as the anchor from day one.

**Capacity-sequencing risk.** If transit capacity isn't expanded ahead of or alongside the charge, the people who stop driving crowd an already-full system, reproducing the same failure pattern that undermines free-transit-alone strategies. *Mitigation:* make the pricing go-live date conditional on a published, binding capacity threshold (a specific bus-frequency or rail-headway target) being met first — turn "backfill capacity" from an intention into an operational gate.

**Measurement and definitional risk.** Without an agreed definition of "commuter car journey," a baseline, and a measurement method, the city can make real progress and still be unable to prove it in year three — and that ambiguity itself becomes a political liability. *Mitigation:* define the metric, baseline, and measurement approach in the enabling policy itself, before launch, so success or failure is falsifiable.

**Political-durability and revenue-integrity risk.** A charge's revenue-recycling promise can be quietly redirected during a budget shortfall, or a change in city administration can reverse or water down the program before its effects fully materialize — again, this has actually happened in the largest, best-resourced real-world example. *Mitigation:* this risk can't be fully engineered away, but it can be structurally reduced by legally earmarking revenue into a locked account rather than a routine budget line, so redirecting it requires a separate, visible political act rather than a quiet decision.

**Exemption-erosion risk.** Affected businesses and interest groups lobbying for exemptions can shrink the priced population enough to fall well short of the demonstrated effect before any measurement dispute even arises. *Mitigation:* use income-based rebates administered after the fact rather than blanket category exemptions — this preserves the price signal for the general driving population while still protecting the people who genuinely need protection.

**Legitimacy-shock risk.** A single visible operational failure early on — a billing glitch, a confusing zone boundary, a traffic-diversion incident — can end political support for the whole program regardless of how sound the underlying design is. *Mitigation:* run a phased or reduced-charge trial period specifically to surface and fix operational problems while the political cost of failure is still low, accepting a short delay to full effect in exchange for a much lower risk of an early, high-visibility failure.

## 6. Recommendation

Don't select a single intervention. Run a **pricing-anchored, revenue-recycled, sequenced program**: congestion pricing supplies the core mechanism because it's the only one of the three that acts directly on the metric being measured and has real-world evidence landing right inside the 18–25% range the city is targeting; its revenue pre-funds transit-capacity expansion and a connected cycle-lane network; and the relative weight and sequencing of the three levers — how hard to lean on cycling, how fast to move on pricing, how much capacity to build first — is set by the five structural facts about the specific city: its baseline car-mode-share and transit headroom, its density/geography/commute-distance profile, its existing bike-network connectivity, its fiscal capacity and farebox dependence, and its political capital and equity exposure.

The key insight worth carrying forward is that the question's own framing — pick one of three — is itself the biggest hidden assumption in the whole decision, and it doesn't survive scrutiny: free transit's mechanism acts mainly on people who weren't driving in the first place, cycle lanes' ceiling is set by a geographic fact most cities can't change in three years, and a weighted comparison of all the realistic strategies shows a bundled, pricing-anchored program beating every single-lever option on nearly every criterion, robustly enough that no reasonable change in how those criteria are weighted reverses the result.

The honest trade-off to acknowledge: anchoring on pricing buys the strongest and fastest mechanism at the cost of the weakest political-durability and equity profile of the three raw levers, and the mitigations needed to fix that (revenue earmarking, income-based rebates rather than blanket exemptions, capacity-first sequencing) will themselves shrink the realized effect somewhat below the best-case 18–25% range — meaning a well-designed program should expect to land nearer the lower half of that range, not its ceiling, especially in its first year or two. And regardless of which combination is chosen, the city cannot actually verify whether it hit "20%" until it defines what that number means — which trips count, what baseline it's measured against, and whether it's a relative or absolute figure — so that definitional work has to happen at the same time as the intervention decision, not after the fact.

## Why the question is harder than it looks

The stated goal — cut *commuter car journeys* by 20% in three years — is more specific than it sounds. It is not "reduce emissions," "cut congestion," "improve equity," or "grow transit ridership." Those four goals are what free transit, congestion pricing, and cycle lanes are usually justified by, and all three interventions can look successful against them while doing very little to the actual metric in question. A city that makes transit free and sees ridership jump 14% has not necessarily put a single car driver on a bus — if most of those new riders used to walk, the emissions and equity numbers can improve while the car-commute number barely moves.

It's also worth flagging that "cut commuter car journeys by 20%" isn't yet a fully specified target — does "commuter" mean only home-to-work trips? Does a carpool passenger count as removed? Relative or absolute? This has to be pinned down alongside the intervention choice, or the city won't be able to tell in three years whether it succeeded.

## 1. Is "choose one" a false framing?

Largely, yes — this is the single most important move in the analysis. The three interventions act on different parts of the same system (congestion pricing prices the trip itself; free transit cuts the cost of one substitute; cycle lanes improve the quality of a different substitute), and nothing prevents doing all three. Real-world pricing schemes (Stockholm, London) are rarely deployed alone — they're typically paired with pre-funded transit or active-travel investment. A weighted comparison across pricing-alone, free-transit-alone, cycle-lanes-alone, and a sequenced bundle shows the bundle beating every single-lever option on nearly every criterion, robustly enough that no reasonable reweighting flips the result.

The one case where "pick exactly one" is the right frame: genuine scarcity of political/administrative capacity, where a city can only credibly execute one major policy change in three years.

## 2. Mechanism, requirements, and failure modes

**Free transit** — removes cost of the substitute. Works only if drivers (not existing walkers/cyclists) are the ones responding. Tallinn's fare-free rollout is the clearest cautionary data point: ridership jumped, but walking trips collapsed ~40% while car use fell only modestly, and average car-trip distance *increased*. Also creates a lasting fiscal hole (fares typically cover 30–60% of operating costs) that can degrade service — and increase car use — over time if unfunded.

**Congestion pricing** — prices the car trip directly, the only mechanism that doesn't depend on someone discovering a substitute first. Stockholm and London both produced 18–25% reductions in priced-zone vehicle trips within the first year — a 20% target sits squarely inside demonstrated results, not past them. Failure modes are political, not mechanical: NYC's program took ~6 years from legislation to launch and was nearly cancelled days before going live. Needs transit capacity headroom to absorb diverted trips, or backlash follows.

**Protected cycle lanes** — improves quality/safety of an existing substitute. Ceiling is set by geography: practical cycling range is roughly 5–8km, shrunk further by climate/topography, and a single corridor does little without network connectivity. A rough sizing check (a third to half of commutes within range, 5–15% conversion over a partial 3-year network) yields something like a 1–8 percentage-point contribution — real, but nowhere near sufficient alone.

## 3. Decision framework — what should route the choice

Five structural facts about the city should set the weighting/sequencing:

1. **Baseline car mode-share and transit headroom** — room to price hard only exists if displaced trips have somewhere to go.
2. **Density, geography, commute-distance distribution** — determines how much weight cycling can realistically carry.
3. **Existing bike-network connectivity** — partial networks complete (and pay off) faster than starting from zero.
4. **Fiscal capacity and farebox dependency** — determines whether free transit is affordable without gutting service.
5. **Political capital, legal authority, equity exposure** — determines how fast pricing can actually launch, and whether it survives once launched.

Rule of thumb: high car share + slack transit + a legible zone + existing tolling authority → lead with pricing. Long commutes/harsh climate → downweight cycling, lean on pricing + capacity. Weak political capital or no tolling authority → sequence transit/cycling first, build the legal case for pricing in parallel, accept a longer runway.

## 4. The three-year constraint

None of the three wins on both speed and strength. Free transit switches on fast but is weak and slow to move car trips. Cycle lanes need years to reach network effects. Pricing's bottleneck is legal/political runway, not construction — potentially consuming most of a three-year window if new legislation is needed. The implication: don't sequence these levers one after another — start transit-capacity and cycle-lane work immediately on existing authority while building the legal case for pricing in parallel.

## 5. Pre-mortem: how this fails

- **Authorization eats the clock** — mitigate by running legal/procurement work in parallel with capacity-building, not after.
- **Capacity crowding** — make the pricing go-live date conditional on a published transit-capacity threshold being met first.
- **Undefined metric** — fix baseline/definition in the enabling policy before launch, or success is unfalsifiable.
- **Revenue diversion / political reversal** — legally earmark revenue into a locked account, not a routine budget line.
- **Exemption creep** — use income-based rebates, not blanket category exemptions, to preserve the price signal.
- **Early operational stumble kills legitimacy** — run a phased/reduced-charge trial to surface glitches while the political cost of failure is still low.

## 6. Recommendation

Don't pick one. Run a **pricing-anchored, revenue-recycled, sequenced program**: congestion pricing supplies the core mechanism (the only lever acting directly on the metric, with real-world results landing right inside the 18–25% target range), its revenue pre-funds transit capacity and a connected cycle network, and the five structural variables above set the relative weight and pace of each piece for the specific city.

The trade-off worth being honest about: anchoring on pricing buys the strongest, fastest mechanism at the cost of the weakest political-durability and equity profile of the three, and the mitigations needed to fix that will themselves shave the realized effect below pricing's best-case ceiling — expect the lower half of the 18–25% range in year one or two, not the top. And none of this is measurable until the city defines what "20%" actually means.
